verbs.note: Irregular: the most common verb in the language; each tense uses its own stem.

forms.english: I am already on the way.
Where are you now?
Where is your car?
We are in the office all day today.
Which floor are you on now?
The children are in the yard.
Tomorrow I will be at home.
Where will you be in the evening?
The weather will be good.
Yesterday I was at the seaside.
Where were you yesterday?
The film was interesting.

verbs.note: Indirect verb: the owner is in the dative case (მე მაქვს — me makvs, მას აქვს — mas akvs).

forms.english: Today I have a lot of time.
Do you have a pen?
This phone has a good camera.
We have a small flat.
How many books do you have?
The children have an exam tomorrow.
Tomorrow I will have more time.
Soon you will have a new job.
The director will soon have free time.
Yesterday I had a day off.
Did you have a good day?
Giorgi had a birthday yesterday.

verbs.note: Indirect verb: the wanter is in the dative case; everyday Georgian mostly uses the present and past.

forms.english: I want a coffee.
What do you want?
Grandmother wants to go to the village.
We want to go to the cinema in the evening.
Do you want tea or coffee?
The children want sweets.
I really wanted to see you.
Why did you want to leave?
Nino wanted to buy a new laptop.

verbs.note: Exceptional: the knower is in the ergative case even in the present and imperfect (მან იცის — man itsis, მან იცოდა — man itsoda); the future flips to a dative construction (მას ეცოდინება — mas etsodineba).

forms.english: I know a little Georgian.
Do you happen to know the password?
Dato already knows this story.
We don't know the exact answer yet.
Do you know what is happening tomorrow?
The students already know everything.
Soon I will know the answer.
Tomorrow you will know the result.
Levan will definitely know about that.
I did not know that back then.
You knew, didn't you?
Tamar knew nothing about this.

verbs.note: Indirect verb: the lover is in the dative case (მე მიყვარს — me miq'vars, მას უყვარს — mas uq'vars).

forms.english: I love Georgian music.
Do you love khachapuri?
The child loves chocolate ice cream very much.
We love relaxing at the sea in the summer.
Do you love Georgian wine?
Georgians love hosting guests.
I will always love this city.
You will always love this song.
Mother will always love him.
As a child I loved fairy tales.
Did you love sports before?
Grandma loved hot tea.

verbs.note: The three tenses use different roots: დი- (di-) in the present, -ვალ/-ვა (-val/-va) in the future, -ვედ/-ვიდ (-ved/-vid) in the past.

forms.english: I am going to work.
Where are you going?
The bus goes to the center.
We are going to Batumi tomorrow morning.
Are you going to the market?
The neighbors are going to the village to rest.
Tomorrow I will go to Tbilisi.
Will you go with us?
The bus will leave at exactly five o'clock.
Yesterday I went to the market.
Why didn't you go to the doctor yesterday?
The boss left a little while ago.

verbs.note: Regular pattern: in the past tense the eater takes the ergative case (კატამ შეჭამა — k'at'am shech'ama).

forms.english: I eat fruit for breakfast.
What are you eating?
The cat isn't eating its food.
We are eating lunch out today.
Do you eat meat?
The children are eating apples.
I will eat the whole khachapuri.
Will you eat this cake?
He won't be able to eat such a big pizza alone.
I accidentally ate all the chocolate.
Did you already eat that cake?
The cat ate the fish.

verbs.note: The future and past switch to the root ლევ/ლი — lev/li (დავლევ — davlev, დავლიე — davlie).

forms.english: In the morning I drink coffee.
What are you drinking?
Grandpa drinks coffee every morning.
We always drink good wine on holidays.
Do you drink wine?
My friends rarely drink beer.
I will drink a glass of water.
Will you drink tea with me?
The patient will take this medicine in the evening.
I drank too much wine last night.
Have you already drunk your coffee?
The guest drank only one glass.

verbs.note: A model regular verb: the და- (da-) preverb marks the future and past (დავწერ — davts'er, დავწერე — davts'ere).

forms.english: I am writing a letter to a friend.
Who are you writing to?
The journalist is writing an interesting article.
We are writing an important project now.
What are you writing?
The students are writing an essay.
Tomorrow I will write the letter.
Will you write the answer?
The lawyer will write the statement tomorrow.
Yesterday I wrote a little poem.
When did you write this beautiful poem?
The writer wrote a new novel.

verbs.note: Present uses the -ულობ (-ulob) stem (ვკითხულობ — vk'itkhulob); future and past take the წა- (ts'a-) preverb and ი- (i-) version vowel (წავიკითხავ — ts'avik'itkhav, წავიკითხე — ts'avik'itkhe).

forms.english: In the evening I read a book.
What are you reading?
Grandfather always reads with glasses.
We are reading the news.
Do you read Georgian books?
The children are reading fairy tales.
I will read this book in the summer.
Will you read my letter?
She will read this book on her days off.
Yesterday I read an interesting article.
Did you read this book?
The child read the fairy tale to the end.

verbs.note: Medial -ობ (-ob) verb: future and past take the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვილაპარაკებ — vilap'arak'eb, ვილაპარაკე — vilap'arak'e). 'In a language' is expressed with -ად (-ad: ქართულად — kartulad) or ენაზე (enaze).

forms.english: I am speaking on the phone right now.
Do you speak English?
The director speaks very fast.
We don't talk about politics at all.
What are you talking about?
The colleagues are talking in the meeting room.
Tomorrow I will speak with the director.
Will you talk to him?
The president will speak live on air tomorrow.
Yesterday I talked with my mother.
Did you talk with the doctor?
Only the manager spoke at the meeting.

verbs.note: Covers both 'learn' and 'study (at school/university)'; future and past use the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვისწავლი — vists'avli, ვისწავლე — vists'avle).

forms.english: I am learning Georgian.
Where do you study?
My brother studies at medical school.
We are learning a new program now.
What are you studying?
The children are learning the alphabet.
This year I will learn Georgian well.
Will you learn this poem?
He will learn the German language soon.
Today I learned ten new words.
Where did you learn Georgian?
The student learned a lot at the university.

verbs.note: Dative-subject (inversion) verb: the owner is in the dative and the animate being owned is in the nominative; used for people, animals, and vehicles (ქონა — kona covers inanimate things).

forms.english: I have two sisters.
Do you have a dog?
Ana has two older sisters.
We have a dog and a cat in the village.
How many children do you have in your family?
The neighbors have a new dog.
Soon I will have a puppy.
You will have many guests tomorrow.
Elene will soon have guests.
As a child I had a parrot.
Did you have a horse before?
Grandma had five children.

verbs.note: The workhorse 'do / make' verb; the გა- (ga-) preverb marks the future and past (გავაკეთებ — gavak'eteb, გავაკეთე — gavak'ete).

forms.english: I am making lunch right now.
What are you doing?
Mother is making dinner.
We do everything together.
What are you doing tomorrow?
The workers are making a new road.
I will do this tomorrow.
Will you do this job by tomorrow?
The repairman will fix it tomorrow.
I have already done the work.
Did you do the homework?
Mother made a delicious lunch.

verbs.note: Suppletive verb: the present uses the ხედ- (khed-) root (ვხედავ — vkhedav), while the future and past switch to ნახ- (nakh-: ვნახავ — vnakhav, ვნახე — vnakhe).

forms.english: From the window I see mountains.
Do you see that bird?
Grandpa already sees poorly.
From here we see everything.
Do you see the sea?
The neighbors see everything.
Tomorrow I will see my friends.
You will see many acquaintances there.
Giorgi will see the new apartment tomorrow.
Yesterday I saw a beautiful rainbow.
Did you see this photo?
Nino saw her aunt yesterday.

verbs.note: Dative-subject (inversion) verb: მესმის (mesmis) covers both 'I hear' and 'I understand (a language)'; everyday Georgian uses the present and imperfect past (მესმოდა — mesmoda).

forms.english: I hear your voice well.
Can you hear my voice?
Dato understands Georgian well.
We understand you very well.
Children, can you hear my voice?
The tourists understand Russian well.
From afar I could hear a song.
Could you hear the noise from outside?
Grandpa was hard of hearing.

verbs.note: Mirror of წასვლა (ts'asvla) with the მო- (mo-, 'hither') preverb; the suppletive roots change by tense (მოვდივარ — movdivar, მოვალ — moval, მოვედი — movedi).

forms.english: I am coming to you now.
When are you coming home?
The train comes on time.
We are coming by bus.
Are you coming on foot?
The guests are coming in the evening.
Tomorrow I will definitely come.
Will you come to my birthday?
He will come soon.
Yesterday I came late.
Why didn't you come?
Winter came early this year.

verbs.note: Relative intransitive verb: the person or thing awaited goes in the dative (ავტობუსს ველოდები — avt'obuss velodebi); the და- (da-) preverb marks the future and past (დაველოდები — davelodebi, დაველოდე — davelode).

forms.english: I am waiting for the bus.
Who are you waiting for?
She is waiting for an answer.
We are waiting for spring.
Have you been waiting long?
The guests are waiting for a taxi.
I will wait for your call.
Will you wait a little while?
He will wait until the end.
I waited an hour for my friend.
Didn't you wait for him?
He waited a little while.

verbs.note: Present uses the -ულობ (-ulob) stem (ვყიდულობ — vq'idulob); the future and past use the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვიყიდი — viq'idi, ვიყიდე — viq'ide).

forms.english: I buy bread every day.
Where do you buy vegetables?
He buys fruit at the market.
We buy the presents together.
What are you buying?
The neighbors are buying a new apartment.
Tomorrow I will buy the tickets.
Will you buy these shoes?
She will buy a new phone.
Yesterday I bought a warm jacket.
What did you buy at the market?
He bought flowers.

verbs.note: Ditransitive suppletive verb: the recipient stands in the dative; the present uses the ძლევ- (dzlev-) root (ვაძლევ — vadzlev), while the future and past use the მი-ცემ- (mi-tsem-) and მი-ეც- / მი-ს-ც- (mi-ets- / mi-s-ts-) stems for a 3rd-person recipient (მივცემ — mivtsem, მივეცი — mivetsi, მისცა — mistsa).

forms.english: I am giving the dog food.
What are you giving the child?
He gives everyone good advice.
We give the cat milk.
Do you give the patient the medicine?
Parents give children everything.
I will give this book to my brother.
Will you give the money to the child?
Grandmother will give candy to the grandchild.
I gave my old bicycle to my brother.
Who did you give your number to?
He gave the child an apple.

verbs.note: Present ვიღებ (vigheb) is shared with მიღება (migheba, 'to receive'); for აღება (agheba, 'to take, pick up, collect'), the ა- (a-) preverb marks the future and past (ავიღებ — avigheb, ავიღე — avighe).

forms.english: I am taking money out of the bank.
Why are you taking my bag?
He takes a book from the shelf.
In the summer we take a vacation.
Are you taking everything from the table?
They get their pension at the bank.
I will get my salary tomorrow.
Will you answer the phone?
The winner will take the prize.
I picked up the key from the table.
Did you take the key?
He took a glass from the table.

verbs.note: Relative intransitive verb: the person helped stands in the dative (დედას ვეხმარები — dedas vekhmarebi); the და- (da-) preverb marks the future and past (დავეხმარები — davekhmarebi, დავეხმარე — davekhmare).

forms.english: I help my mother in the kitchen.
Who are you helping?
Ana is helping her mother in the kitchen.
We help each other.
Do you help your parents?
The volunteers help many people.
I will help the neighbor with the renovation.
Will you help your brother?
He will help grandma in the garden.
I helped grandma with cleaning.
Why didn't you help your brother?
A passer-by helped the old man.

verbs.note: Medial -ობ (-ob) verb for games and sports (musical instruments use დაკვრა — dak'vra); the future and past take the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვითამაშებ — vitamasheb, ვითამაშე — vitamashe).

forms.english: In the evening I play chess.
Do you play football?
The child is playing in the yard.
On Sundays we play together.
What are you playing?
The girls are playing basketball.
I will play football in the evening.
Will you play with us?
He will play in the final.
Yesterday I played for two hours.
Did you play well?
The team played brilliantly.

verbs.note: Root მღერ- (mgher-); the masdar სიმღერა (simghera) also means 'song', and the future and past take the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვიმღერებ — vimghereb, ვიმღერე — vimghere).

forms.english: I often sing in the bathroom.
You sing very well.
She sings in a choir.
At the supra we sing together.
Do you sing Georgian songs?
The children sing at school.
I will sing at the wedding.
Will you sing for us?
He will sing at the concert.
At the supra I sang three songs.
What did you sing at the concert?
My uncle sang at the supra.

verbs.note: Medial -ავ (-av) verb; the future and past take the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვიცეკვებ — vitsek'veb, ვიცეკვე — vitsek've).

forms.english: I dance in an ensemble.
Do you dance traditional Georgian dances?
Nino dances very well.
At weddings we all dance.
Do you dance the Kartuli?
The girls are dancing on stage.
I will dance at your wedding.
Will you dance with me?
The bride will dance at the wedding.
At the party I danced until morning.
Did you dance a lot yesterday?
He danced the Acharuli.

verbs.note: Medial -ობ (-ob) verb (ვმუშაობ — vmushaob); the future and past take the ი- (i-) version vowel on the მუშავ- (mushav-) stem without a preverb (ვიმუშავებ — vimushaveb, ვიმუშავე — vimushave).

forms.english: I work at a school.
Where do you work?
My father works at a bank.
We work on Saturdays too.
Do you work together?
The builders work a lot.
Tomorrow I will work from home.
Where will you work in the summer?
Giorgi will work tomorrow too.
Yesterday I worked until late.
Did you work a lot today?
The repairman worked all night.

verbs.note: Medial -ობ (-ob) verb (ვცხოვრობ — vtskhovrob); the future and past take the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვიცხოვრებ — vitskhovreb, ვიცხოვრე — vitskhovre).

forms.english: I live in Tbilisi.
Where do you live?
My sister lives in Tbilisi.
We live on the fifth floor.
Have you lived here long?
Grandma and grandpa live in the village.
In the summer, I will live at the summer house.
Where will you live next year?
The student will live in a rental.
I lived in Batumi for five years.
Did you really live in Germany?
My uncle lived in Moscow for a long time.

verbs.note: 'Is asleep / sleeps' is a dative-subject state in the present (მას სძინავს — mas sdzinavs); 'go to sleep / fall asleep' switches to the active-intransitive და-ი-ძინ- (da-i-dzin-) stem in the future and past (დავიძინებ — davidzineb, დავიძინე — davidzine).

forms.english: I don't hear noise when I'm asleep.
It's noon and you're still sleeping?
The cat is asleep on the sofa.
In summer we sleep on the balcony.
Do you sleep in tents?
The children are already asleep.
Today I will go to bed early.
When will you go to sleep?
The child will fall asleep soon.
Yesterday I went to bed late.
What time did you go to sleep?
The child has already fallen asleep.

verbs.note: Medial -ობ (-ob) verb; 'about' something takes the -ზე (-ze) postposition (შენზე ვფიქრობ — shenze vpikrob), and the future and past take the ი- (i-) version vowel without a preverb (ვიფიქრებ — vipikreb, ვიფიქრე — vipikre).

forms.english: I often think about you.
What are you thinking about?
The director is thinking about the new project.
We think so too.
What do you think about this?
Parents always think about their children.
I will think about this tomorrow.
Will you think about my offer?
He will think about this problem later.
I thought a lot and refused.
Did you think about this?
Dato thought the worst.

verbs.note: Dative-subject (inversion) verb: the liker stands in the dative and the thing liked is in the nominative (მე მომწონს — me momts'ons, მას მოსწონს — mas mosts'ons; imperfect მომწონდა — momts'onda).

forms.english: I like this song a lot.
Do you like my new haircut?
The client likes the new design.
We like this city a lot.
Do you like Georgian cuisine?
The children like this game.
Let's see if I will like it.
You will like this film.
Mother will like this present.
As a child I liked winter.
Did you like school?
Grandpa liked old songs.

verbs.note: Dative-subject in the present (მე შემიძლია — me shemidzlia + masdar or optative); the future and past flip to transitive forms (შევძლებ — shevdzleb, შევძელი — shevdzeli, ergative subject in the aorist).

forms.english: I can help financially.
Can you lend me some money?
Dato can do this.
We can do this together.
Can you come tomorrow?
The guests can stay.
I will manage this too.
Will you manage alone?
Giorgi will be able to pass the exam.
In the end I managed it after all.
Were you able to arrive on time?
The doctor was able to save the patient.

verbs.note: Transitive verb with the ი- (i-) version vowel; the და- (da-) preverb marks the future and past (დავიწყებ — davits'q'eb, დავიწყე — davits'q'e). Note transitive იწყებს (its'q'ebs, 's/he starts something') vs. intransitive იწყება (its'q'eba, 'something starts').

forms.english: I start work at nine o'clock.
When do you start studying?
The teacher is starting the lesson.
Today we are starting a new topic.
When do you start the rehearsal?
The neighbors are starting renovations.
From tomorrow I will start exercising.
Will you start a new book?
Nino will start working on Monday.
Yesterday I started a diet.
When did you start learning Georgian?
The child suddenly started crying.
